utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not the Chamber but it's myself who apologises for the late start today. Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you, Your Honour. Case IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Tieger: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Nielsen.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the adjournment yesterday, you were discussing reports by the MUP in the course of discussing the general system of reporting and communications. Before we move on - and I'm going to try today to move as quickly as we possibly can - perhaps we can focus on at least a couple of other methods of communicating by the MUP. And in that connection, perhaps we can turn to tab 46 of binder 2, which contains an article by Glas of 14 May 1992 concerning the security services celebration on 13 May in Banja Luka. Mr. Nielsen, can you tell us what that event was and whether it provided an opportunity for communications by members of the MUP to other parts of the Bosnian Serb political authorities.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This provides me with a very quick opportunity to provide some brief historical background to the Chamber. In the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the 13th of May was a holiday, so to speak, officially known as Security Day. This went back to the 1940s because the 13th of May was the day on which the Yugoslav Communists had formed the first communist police services. So this was in a way -- this particular parade, which is photographed and dealt with in this article, was part of an annual celebration of the security forces in Yugoslavia, the difference here of course being that in 1992 the participants in the parade were all members of the recently established RS Ministry of Internal Affairs. This particular parade was also the debut for a special police unit that had been formed constituting about 160 persons in the CSB Banja Luka and commanded under the authority of Stojan Zupljanin, the chief of CSB Banja Luka. As we can see -- the Chamber will have to turn to the B/C/S original to be able to see this. But the B/C/S original, which is a one-page article, shows several photographs of the parade. It also shows the Minister of Internal Affairs, Mico Stanisic, addressing the assembled audience as well as several political dignitaries. And indeed the text of the article reflects that many political leaders, including at the national, which is to say, the RS level at this point in time, and also at the ARK, Autonomous Region of Krajina level, were present at this -- at this particular occasion. The general message provided by everyone, both the police and the politicians present, as they're quoted in the article, is that the situation in the Banja Luka region is under control and that the police are functioning as they should.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Kupresanin say on that occasion, "With the creation of the police and the Army of the Serbian Republic, the Serbs have become masters of their own territory."

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is indeed correct. And in -- I might point out that in making that statement, Mr. Kupresanin was reflecting a quite important statement made at an earlier stage in the Bosnian Serb Assembly. I'm just going to locate the paragraph in my report. If one looks at paragraph 185 of my report, which is on page 52, I cite Biljana Plavsic already on the 26th of January, 1992 stating that, and I quote: "These are the times until the referendum when the Serbian people must make a state out of its own areas. It is known what the making of a state means. First, the Ministry of Internal Affairs will do whatever necessary to have its own army." As I pointed out yesterday, the Ministry of Internal Affairs in its draft annual report for 1992 was quite proud or -- I can rephrase that, put quite a lot of emphasis on the leading role of the Ministry of Internal Affairs in the early stages of the existence of Republika Srpska. So to go back to the article in tab 46, Mr. Kupresanin's comments are in fact reflective that what was contemplated or anticipated earlier in the year in the Assembly has now been realised in practice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the celebration reflected in the 14 May 1992 Glas article take place the day after the 16th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, which was held in Banja Luka on the 12th of May and presided over by Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. The parade took place, as I noted, on the 13th of May, Security Day, "Dan Belbjednosti" in B/C/S, and this particular occasion it was the day after the 16th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, at which the military of the -- or the Army of Republika Srpska, Vojska Republika Srpska was also established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does the Glas article or the photographs indicate whether or not Mr. Krajisnik was present at the parade?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the Chamber will examine, again, the B/C/S copy, since it is the only one that is -- has the photographs, it can be observed in the photograph on the right-hand side of the page, the second from the top. There is a photograph depicting Momcilo Krajisnik in addition to Radovan Karadzic, Radoslav Brdjanin, I believe Nikola Koljevic, and several other political leaders. I would just also note, because this will be quite important in understanding the functioning of the special unit, that the picture immediately below the picture of Mico Stanisic at the microphone on the left-hand side is a picture of armoured personnel carriers that are being used by the police in the Banja Luka region. It is -- unfortunately, the copy we have here is very poor. It may be useful to look at the original. But I can tell from having looked at the original that on the front of those armoured personnel carriers in Cyrillic capital letters is the word "milicija," or police, as it was known at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the helicopters shown in the photograph above Mr. Stanisic's photograph, are those helicopters, belonging to the RS police or military authorities?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The helicopters --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just in relation to that, I think it would be helpful if -- and it's just a simple question: Do you have any information in relation to those helicopters, rather than leading, I would have thought, on Mr. Tieger's part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't want to get into the nuances of practice in whatever jurisdiction we come from, but when working with an expert, at least in the jurisdiction I come from, that's an entirely appropriate question and -- and doesn't lead Mr. Nielsen in one direction or another. And I think this is not the time to fall back on the formalities of a system that is not in place here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, Mr. Tieger, it would not have cost you any additional time to ask what the expert witness knows about who owned the helicopters -- three. There are three. I'm not asking you to ask how many helicopters there are, but you could have asked him what he knows about where these helicopters come from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, can you tell us anything about those helicopters?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would refer first to the caption that is in the newspaper below the photograph, which states - and I will translate the B/C/S - it states: "Helicopters of the security services." In the usage -- B/C/S usage at the time, that is a clear reference that they are police helicopters and not military helicopters. I would also in further answering that question refer the Court to the section of my report in which I discuss the establishment of special police units in the RS MUP that starts on page 62, and there I have cited documentation that shows that the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army at the time, agreed to fulfil a request for equipment by Stojan Zupljanin so that that unit that we see on these photographs could be equipped. And having seen the actual request from Zupljanin as well as the JNA's response, it was the General Kukanjac who eventually granted the request, that did indeed include a request for both armoured personnel carriers and helicopters that we see in this particular article..

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, let's turn next to another form of communication between --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have three, or at least two questions to ask. Since I would have to backtrack and since things seem to be moving rather fast, I would just like to ask the witness to specify a couple of things. With regard to those reports we discussed yesterday, the reports that had to be submitted daily to the hierarchy and even go as far as the ministry itself, in the course of your research, have you uncovered any of -- any of those reports? Have you analysed them? Could you tell us anything about the contents of those reports? Because we have seen the model, as it were. You showed it to us yesterday. But have you been able to analyse any of the actual reports that had been submitted to the ministry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have been in a position or I should say I was in a position while I was still employed in this office to examine many - and when I use the word "many," I mean dozens and dozens, more than 100 - of such reports that were filed in 1992. I've examined both reports that were filed by the CSBs to the ministry and also the next level, that is to say, the collated version, the reports that the ministry then composed based on the reports it received every day at noon from the CSBs. I compiled in the course of my analysis a binder and a spreadsheet containing, again, dozens of reference -- dozens of examples of these reports, and I can inform the Court that generally speaking the emphasis on those reports is on the police's extensive involvement in combat activities during 1992 rather than on traditional police activities per se, combatting crime, establishing order in various neighbourhoods, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And my second question is this: We see these police units cropping up and they seem to resemble military units rather more than police officers. Would it mean that all regular activity carried out by regular police went by the wayside? Let me explain this. We have got a ministry which is in charge of internal affairs. This ministry organises and reorganises and restructures the police force at the municipality level or at the regional level. And on the basis of the examples that you've shown to us, apparently this police force takes on an almost military aspect and role. Would it mean that all the traditional tasks and roles of the police were simply discarded and forgotten about because they were concentrated on military aspects and goals only?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that would be a very correct observation. The draft annual report -- I will quote the paragraph 338 of my report, where I quote directly from the draft annual report. "Since the very beginning of the war, almost the entire available personnel of the organs for internal affairs have been involved in war activities for the liberation of occupied territories and the protection of liberated Serbian territories. This in good measure also persists today." That is a quote from a report that was produced in January 1993. That situation obtained for the entire period from April 1992 until the end of 1992 and is in fact, if I may refer back to the 14 April steering council meeting that we had a chance to see yesterday, I believe it was Cedomir Kljajic, the under-secretary for public security who already at that very early stage expressed concern that the police would be too busy with combat activities to actually do any policing. This statement is a statement that appears again and again or a concern that appears again and again in the documents, and in particular it appears at a very important meeting of the entire leadership of the Ministry of Internal Affairs that takes place on the 11th of July, 1992 in Belgrade, at which point, among many other comments, the minister and his subordinates state that they don't understand why, for example, the police, to quote one participant, are in the trenches while the army is directing traffic. And one of the main conclusions coming out of that meeting was that the police needed to find a way to extract itself from combat activities and spend more time on policing. The draft annual report shows that they did not succeed in doing so by the end of 1992. And I'll finally note that -- I see we don't have the list of tabs in front of me here. But there is a document from the minister on the 15th of May, 1992, two days -- or actually one day after this article in which he specifically orders that the entire ministry be reorganised into "ratne jedinice," war units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, if you'd allow me just a brief question in relation to one of Judge Hanoteau's questions. When you say the bottom line of the reports to the ministry and also the -- then the condensed reports compiled of this was about the role of the MUP in the -- in combat activities, do you understand by "combat activities" the real combat, that is, combatants against combatants, or would you also include other phenomena, as we have seen in your report, about expulsions and deportations, or is it just combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It includes combat in the strict military sense of the word with other armed forces of an opposing side, and this was the case of -- in particular for the special detachment that was led by Milenko Karisik, and I might note had at its disposal weapons up to and including 120-millimetre mortars. These are very substantial military weapons, not usually employed by police forces. And the reports as a whole for the ministry in 1992 show that the police participated extensively on a daily basis, and the figures are included in the draft annual report, on the battlefield with -- together with first the TO and JNA forces in the period before 12 May 1992 and thereafter in coordination with the VRS, the Army of Republika Srpska. However, to answer Your Honour's question, they also participated in what are referred to, I believe, usually in the English translation as "mopping-up activities." These are operations of a low-intensity conflict, post-combat operations that could include and did include disarming the remaining "enemy population."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say "disarming the remaining enemy population," that could -- could be understood as we take their arms but we leave them where they are. Is that what you intended to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. As a matter of fact, Your Honour, in the report I detail and cite a large number of documents that indicate that in the course of those mopping-up operations a very large number of people, thousands of people, were rounded up by the police and the military, sometimes both working jointly, sometimes the two working separately, but with the goal -- or not with the goal but, rather, with the result that the -- that a very large number of persons that the police in fact later determined to be not -- non-combatants essentially were rounded up and placed in detention facilities in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen that. The role of the MUP in detention facilities is clearly described very much focussing on, I would say, Prijedor, and then first Omarska, Keraterm, Trnopolje, and then later - what is it - Manjaca. But I'm -- my question is very much focussing on -- on what exactly was in these reports because these sources you use there, also the sources where you describe the role of the MUP in the armed forces, the sources are not always, and very often not, the reports to the ministry. They are very often reports at a lower level or other sources. I'm specifically interested to know whether that part of the activities, as you said "mopping-up," not real combat activities but, as you described them, low-intensive post-combat activities, to what extent do they appear in these reports? So it's not whether they took place but to what extent are they described in the reports? Because I saw where you are talking about reports. Sometimes it's -- it's language as -- that people voluntarily wanted to leave because they felt closer to the Muslim people and therefore wanted to -- not to stay where they were. That's, of course, not mopping up, that's not driving people out of their homes. So I wonder to what extent that explicitly appears in these reports. It's also a very long question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do understand Your Honour's question. I would just ask if Your Honour could instruct me with regard to these reports, is Your Honour referring to the daily bulletins that Judge Hanoteau mentioned earlier?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I meant them all. I'm mainly interested in reports that finally were sent to the higher levels. That is, you have told us that reports were sent on a regular basis to the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and you have also mentioned the daily bulletins that were sent to the president of the Presidency, I think, and you also talked about special reports; I think 90 to the Prime Minister and 80 to the Presidency and its members. So I'm interested in how specific this information reached these levels.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the case that by the 11th of July, 1992, which is the meeting in Belgrade to which I referred, which was attended by the minister and all of the other leading officials of the ministry, the large-scale rounding-up of persons and their placement in detention facilities was certainly discussed at that meeting. I mentioned that in paragraph 261. And indeed it was noted that the ministry was involved in the operation of those detention camps and that the conditions in these camps were very bad. However, Stojan Zupljanin, who was the person together with Andrija Bjelosevic, who was the chief of CSB Doboj, both of them mentioned this phenomenon, tended to place the responsibility for these large-scale round-ups on the VRS. Specifically Zupljanin said that, as I state, "The VRS in the ARK area demanded the collection of large numbers of Muslims in established undefined camps which had been placed under MUP control." That's one instance that -- in which certainly the top of the ministry was aware of this. I discuss in that same section, in paragraph 263, further communications from Zupljanin to Stanisic and in particular a communication in which Zupljanin advises the minister that they have established three categories of detainees. And he suggests what might be done with those three categories. I do want to note that already at an earlier stage, that is to say, at the end of May, Simo Drljaca in Prijedor municipality had agreed to a Crisis Staff request or order to establish a detention facility known as Omarska, and he certainly reported on that phenomenon, the existence of that facility and the police's control of it to Zupljanin. I cannot say at this point whether Zupljanin in the period between the end of May and early July reported on the involvement of Drljaca's police station in the operation of Omarska. I do not have any specific document to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if I may just -- if I look at paragraph 261, of course it's clear that they're talking about the collection of large numbers of Muslims, but that does not say whether these were large numbers of Muslim combatants or Muslim civilians or what else. And then in 263, you refer to the three categories. The first is persons suspected of commission of criminal acts. Okay. Well, one could imagine without committing a war crime or a crime against humanity that you detain someone who is suspected of the commission of criminal acts. The second would you say suspected of aiding and abetting, those from the first category. And then the third category was compiled of adult males concerning whom the service had not to date gathered any security relevant data. But that's all persons, persons, adult males. It's not driving civilians out of their houses, including wives and children. So I'm interested to know in what detail, information about, as you said, and including mopping-up, which I consider not -- consider not to be arresting criminals - whether they were or not is another matter - but I'm trying to find out where exactly do we see in the reports all women and children of this village were brought to that camp or -- if -- if that ever happened, of course. And, of course, we heard some evidence to the extent that it was not just these fake three categories but there was more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are two brief observations that I would make in response to Your Honour's question. The first one is that as of the -- it's either the 26th -- I believe it is the 26th of May that Drljaca reports to Zupljanin that he is aware that in the course of mopping-up operations a large number of what he calls "the innocent Muslim population" of surrounding villages of Prijedor have been killed. That is a document that I do not cite in the report but I am -- I am prepared to produce that to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Zupljanin is at what level at that time? The regional level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He is the regional chief of the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, my question focuses on -- on a higher level. I mean, Zupljanin was -- was -- the Banja Luka region, SAO Krajina, not -- not Pale, not government, not Presidency, not ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, besides the discussions that took place on the 11th of July to which I already referred, certainly in the period between April and -- and 11 July you do not see in the reports to the minister, or indeed in the reports that we referred to yesterday up to the higher levels, references to women and children being rounded up in mopping-up operations to -- on that specific point. That is not reflected in those documents. It is reflected in a -- or a knowledge of that fact is reflected in a number of intercepted phone conversations made by senior police officials in the Sarajevo area with respect to events at Ilidza, Dobrinja, and other Sarajevo suburbs. But there is, as far as I've been able to determine, no documents and -- and very little trace in the daily bulletins for 1992 as a whole of references to detention facilities and mopping-up operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for those answers. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to follow up on a couple of the questions by the Court. Mr. Nielsen, you referred to the 11 July meeting and the comments of Mr. Zupljanin anyone and Mr. Bjelosevic. Mr. Stanisic was present at that 11 July meeting I believe you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Stanisic -- or was a report made following up from that meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a -- a report sent out pursuant to the main conclusions of that meeting. And that report was sent out by Stanisic with orders for action to be taken with respect to the main -- main conclusions of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that a report on -- entitled "Report on some aspects of the work done to date and the tasks ahead," dated 17 July 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it state in part: "The army, Crisis Staffs, and War Presidencies have requested that the army round up or capture as many Muslim civilians as possible and they leave such undefined camps to internal affairs organs. The conditions in some of these camps are poor. There is no food. Individuals sometimes do not observe international norms," et cetera?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to whom was that or to which bodies was that report sent?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I please have the document produced?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, this document has been previously introduced into evidence as P447 and P447.1, with a translation; also P529, tab 454, and it's also in the Treanor materials.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm just wondering if there are copies available for -- from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, it's on Sanction, is it? Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The particular copy -- the B/C/S copy that I have in front of me, bearing ERN 03246855, I think it would be useful if I could please display it on the ELMO. I'd like to draw the Court's attention to the handwriting on the upper right-hand side of the title page. It starts that this report was given to the president of the Presidency and the president of the government; that is to say, the Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the ciscenje or mopping-up or cleansing operations, however they've been interpreted in the English, to which you referred in response to one of the Court's questions, could I ask you to turn to tab 23, the RS MUP draft annual report. Can I direct your attention first, please, to page 5 of the English translation, the second paragraph. And the English translation reads: "Apart from taking part in armed conflict --"

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just -- sorry to interrupt, but could we also have the B/C/S reference for Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's page 3 -- or the end of page 2, Mr. Tieger. It's just above where it's underlined "Semberija Majevica." And that appears right on top of page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Much obliged. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, the English translation reads: "Apart from taking part in armed conflict at the front line, the police indirectly took part in mopping up remaining enemy groups and individuals, secured the free territory, provided security for transports of weapons and ammunition," et cetera. Is there any aspect -- based on your reading of the B/C/S, is that an entirely correct translation of that particular sentence?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is a correct translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It indicates: "The police indirectly took part in mopping up"?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pardon me. I'm looking here in the -- if -- on the B/C/S copy, which is -- the pages FI201281, there is a significant translation error in the last line on that page. It's the third word from the left-hand side, which -- I'll read it in B/C/S, is "neposredno." That should be translated as "directly," not "indirectly."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm seeking confirmation from the booth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Exact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much for your confirmation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we could turn also to page 23 of the report. I'm sorry, pardon me. It's page 18. And perhaps you'd be good enough as to -- when you find that, to identify the corresponding B/C/S page.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be starting on -- depending on which paragraph it is, it should be on page FI21299 or FI201300.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And that paragraph indicates that: "In addition to other tasks, it should be stressed that police activity was directed at disarming paramilitary formations and individuals and at finding and seizing illegally-held weapons and ammunition, explosive devices and the like. Important tasks of the police in cooperation with the army were in mopping up the terrain of inserted terrorist and sabotage groups and neutralising armed rebellions organised by Muslim Croat extremists (Prijedor, Kotor Varos, Novi Grad, Kljuc, Sanski Most, Jajce, Bihac, Teslic, Gornji Vakuf, Kupres, Knezevo, Mrkonjic Grad, Han Pijesak, Pale, and other SJBs)." And is that another reflection of the police participation in ciscenje operations in various municipalities across the territory of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is an accurate reflection. And as in other cases, the paragraph that we have just seen in the draft annual report is an accurate reflection of the numerous reports filed throughout the summer and -- well, particularly throughout the summer of 1992 with respect to police involvement in such mopping-up operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the -- at the same time, Mr. Tieger, you may have noticed I was mainly interested in what was known at the time. Now you have drawn our attention to a report, which I take it could not -- well, the date is the 1st of January, 1993, although it describes the events in 1992. I was not mainly interested in the events that happened but on -- whether, how quickly, and how that was reported to the highest levels. And if Mr. Nielsen now says, Well, this annual report, of which we know that it could never have been there before the 1st of January, 1993, reflects what we find in the other reports, you'll understand that that would need more exploration, then, to see what appears in these other reports, because on an earlier question Mr. Nielsen told us that there was not much of direct participation in -- in detention and mopping-up in those reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I understand, Your Honour. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore I find myself a bit uncertain after the events, to report it. Mr. Nielsen now says that report reflects what was earlier reported. So we are very much interested in what was -- and that's most of the questions of the last half an hour, is exactly what was reported at those earlier stages up to the highest levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's quite true. Although I understood there seemed to be a question about the nature of the ciscenje operations and -- and their link to disarming, and I thought it would be useful for the Court to see the places in which they occurred, because the Court has considerable information about what happened in those locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Mr. Tieger, I'd like to put a question to the witness. Since we are talking about these operations led by the MUP, by the police services, I would like you to provide us with some indication as to the way in which this police force was involved in this sort of mission. Who issued orders? At what level would the initiative be taken? Has it transpired from your research? I've read on page 55 of your report in para 192 you are saying: [In English] "The ARK Crisis Staff declared that the Crisis Staffs are now the highest organ of authority in the municipality." [Interpretation] And somewhere else - I can't find the passage right now - but you did say that within that Crisis Staff there were representatives of both the police force and the armed forces. Now, if you have a combat operation or any other sort of operation, for that matter, and it is led and carried out by that police force, well, have you managed to establish in the course of your work who was actually at the origin of this, who issued the original orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the example Your Honour just referred to, with the ARK Crisis Staff, the ARK Crisis Staff gave general orders starting in May 1992 to all subordinate Crisis Staffs to start disarming paramilitary groups and the civilian population. These -- there were a series of deadlines set for the compliance with those disarmament orders, and that disarmament order as well as the subsequent deadlines and subsequent orders were disseminated to the Municipal Crisis Staffs throughout ARK. It bears mentioning that Stojan Zupljanin, as chief of CSB Banja Luka, was a member of the ARK Crisis Staff and later what was called the ARK War Staff. At the municipal level in each municipality the chief of the public security station was a member of the Municipal Crisis Staff. And as Your Honour noted, there were also members or representatives of the military on those Crisis Staffs. What one sees regularly throughout the summer of 1992 is that the Crisis Staffs, both at the regional and the municipal level, issue orders that involve actions that have to be taken by the police. The police then proceed through their own chain of command to act on such orders. For example, if the ARK Crisis Staff gave an order to disarm the civilian population in the ARK region, someone such as Simo Drljaca, as chief of SJB Prijedor, actually received the order twice. He would be part of carrying or transmitting that order in the Municipal Crisis Staff, of which he was a member, but he would also receive the same order more or less from his superior in the ministry, Stojan Zupljanin, who would be passing it on directly because he had attended the meetings and was implementing the decisions of the ARK Crisis Staff. And it is from those orders that we then subsequently see in the documents, in the police reports, that actions have been taken pursuant to those orders, and those actions do include these mopping-up operations that we've been discussing. Such actions are often carried out in coordination with the police. I just want to clarify one point. In my previous answer, when I referred to the cumulative nature of the draft annual report and saying that it was reflective of documents kept and filed by the police in the summer of 1992, I was referring to documents between Stojan Zupljanin and Drljaca or between SJBs generally and CSBs and the minister and not specifically to the communications in the summer of 1992 between the ministry and the Presidency or the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd just like you to complete my question in the following way: When you wrote that "On the 18th of May, 1992 the ARK -- the Crisis Staff declared," and so on and so on, could you now clarify the actual structure, the organisation of that Crisis Staff. Was there a kind of Chief of Staff or the Main Staff at the level of the republic or a regional organisation or a municipal organisation? Do you have any information about that? I'm not clear about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am fully prepared to speak about the relationship between the police and the Crisis Staffs and about the orders that the police received and transmitted; however, I'm not an expert on the Crisis Staff. I believe the -- the Chamber had a report from one of my colleagues specifically on the Crisis Staffs, and it would be, I think, superfluous and unnecessary on my part to comment further on -- on the particular internal operations of the Crisis Staffs. Indeed, I would note that most of my own views regarding the Crisis Staffs are formed based on that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. When you said that the decision had been taken at the Crisis Staff level, and as far as the objectives to be achieved and the operations to be carried out were concerned, well, can we say it was included within the discussions within the Crisis Staff? Did you see that in terms of references to that in any documents, in terms of documenting that decision-making process?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I have been able to see and I have read many Crisis Staff minutes, both at the regional level and also at the municipal level, is very frequent mentions to the police and activities that the police are to carry out. And what one can also observe is that orders that are formulated by the ARK Crisis Staff at the regional level are transmitted, as I stated, not only through the police chain of command but also through the Municipal Crisis Staffs. Sometimes -- it is interesting to observe, sometimes, and on this particular issue of disarming, the wording will differ slightly; that is to say, the ARK Crisis Staff, I believe -- we have in one of the tabs the order to disarm the population from the ARK Crisis Staff that I cite, in which they warn the population of -- and again, I want to double-check the -- the document, but I believe it's of the most strict consequences if they do not comply with the order. It's interesting to note that at -- in Kljuc municipality, the same order, which involves handing over weapons to the police and to the local public security station, actually warns the population of catastrophic consequences if they do not comply with this same order, to disarm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just following up on one of your responses to the Court's questions, you referred to the disarming order that was set in motion at the ARK level. And perhaps I can ask you to look at tab 65. Now, first of all, looking -- tab 65 is an order for general mobilisation. At least that's the heading on the tab. Looking at item number 5 in that order or decision, does that reflect the order for disarming -- or one variation of that order for disarming to which you referred to earlier?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. And it does use the term "strictest measures" in describing the possible consequences of not handing over weapons before the deadline.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did that order originate with -- first of all, I should note that it's signed by the secretary of the Regional Secretariat for National Defence. Did that order originate with the Autonomous Region of Krajina or was it the product of a decision from a higher level?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order that is being given at the level of the Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina refers in the introductory paragraph to the decision of the Ministry of National Defence of 16 April 1992, which is a higher legal instance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Minister of National Defence was Mr. Subotic?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he issue that order of 16 April 1992, which is referred to at the top of the document at tab 65?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in connection with your response to a question about Crisis Staffs, you indicated to Judge Hanoteau that one of your colleagues had testified in -- had submitted a report that focussed in particular on that issue. This Court has also heard testimony from Mr. Treanor, who dealt with a variety of issues at the republic level. Nevertheless, I want to ask you at least a couple of questions about some of the material that may already have been covered in much more detail by Mr. Treanor. First of all, are you familiar with the 28 February Law on National Defence?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us in general terms what that provides and its connection to any other legislative acts that bear on the -- the hierarchy of the police, that is, who has authority to order the police at particular times.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that in both the Law on National Defence and the later Law on Defence, which comes once the VRS has been formed - I believe it's Article 6 and 7 of both laws that refer to the cooperation between the military and police units during that -- during combat operations and specifically provide for the possibility of subordinating police units to military units during combat operations. That is also something that is reflected in an order issued on 15 May by Mico Stanisic, the minister, in which he discusses the temporary subordination of command for police units to VRS units in the course of immediate combat operations. He does make it clear, however, that the ultimate responsibility of those police units will remain with him, as the minister. And it should be stated at this point that generally speaking the police of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, together with the VRS, were considered as the armed forces of the RS in the period following the 16th Assembly Session on the 12th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know whether or not a state of war or imminent threat of war was declared in -- by Republika Srpska authorities in 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that such a state of imminent threat of war was declared by the National Security Council on the 15th [realtime transcript read in error "5th"] of April, 1992 at a session of that body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the February 28th Law on National Defence provide that during a state of war or imminent threat of war the president or, if there's a collective body, the Presidency orders the use of the police?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first, I see in the LiveNote that I said it's the 5th of April. I did state the 15th of April. Such a -- a provision with regards to the police and the president's or the Presidency's command of the police is actually found in Article 81 of the Constitution, which provides for the police to be commanded by the Presidency or president during time of imminent threat of war, and it's also found in the Law on National Defence. In addition, since I did mention Article 81, I believe it's important to note that since we discussed yesterday the subordination of the ministry, like other ministries, to the government, it's significant to note here that the ministry during a period of imminent threat of war is not subordinate to the Assembly but, rather, to the Presidency, which is empowered during a time of imminent threat of war to take decisions that are normally in the competency of the Assembly. So that is the legal basis, as it were, for the -- the situation that I just discussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If we could -- there's been some discussion about the disarming operations. And let me just turn to a couple of tabs that address that issue. First quickly to tab 25, please. First of all, is tab 25 an order from Stojan Zupljanin sent to all the public security stations in the -- within the jurisdiction of the CSB Banja Luka in response to the May 4th document we looked at earlier, including -- there seems to be a verbatim reflection of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just before we proceed with that -- sorry to interrupt in relation to -- at that point. But in fact Mr. Krajisnik tells me he does not have tab 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then he should --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He's probably looking at -- he's probably looking at binder 1. It's the beginning of binder 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Binder 2 starts with 25. Binder 1 ends with 24.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I think Mr. Krajisnik has found it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Nielsen, I just wanted to identify that document and ask you if that was the response of chief of the CSB Banja Luka, Stojan Zupljanin, to the ARK order disseminating it to the SJBs.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document in tab 25 is essentially a verbatim transmission of the document we viewed earlier, the 4 May document, by Stojan Zupljanin to the chiefs of all subordinate public security stations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And if you can turn quickly to tab 31. I think that's a reflection of something you mentioned earlier as well. And if you could tell us what that is, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tab 31 is a dispatch from Simo Drljaca, who has signed the -- the B/C/S copy, dated the 31 of July, 1992, in which he has stated that he has received a dispatch from CSB Banja Luka, and he then transmits a verbatim copy of this dispatch that he has received. And that dispatch in turn refers back to the -- the document that we had in tab 30 and asks the SJB to provide information on weapons, munitions, and other explosive means which have been confiscated from paramilitary formations and individuals since the beginning of the disarming campaign and ending with the 31st of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that connection, can we turn next to tab 32, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tab 32 is a report or dispatch dated 2nd of August, 1992 from Drljaca's SJB in Prijedor to Banja Luka. This particular copy is not signed by Drljaca. It's actually signed for him. And in it, referring back to the 31 July dispatch, we now have a list here of, again, weapons, munitions, and other explosive means that have been confiscated in the course of the disarming campaign.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that list includes 17 automatic rifles, 7 M-48s, 185 hunting rifles, and so on; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And turning quickly to tab 10 in binder 1. That is a nine-month report of the Prijedor SJB for the year 1992. And if I could ask you to turn to page 4 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be page 00633750 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the paragraph that begins, after the heading "Participation of the members of the station in combat operations," does the report detail the activities of the police in connection with what are called combat activities in various locations throughout the Prijedor municipality, and does it further describe the ciscenje activities or ciscenje operations that took place after these operations and in which the police engaged?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This section, "Participation of the members of the station in" -- or actually there is again a discrepancy between the B/C/S and the original. The actual B/C/S original says "Participation of members of the service in combat activities," not "members of the station."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we take that from you, we usually rely on the services of our interpreters. Could you please read the B/C/S so that we can get confirmation that your translation is the right one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Participation of the members of the service in combat activity."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... of our translators. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This paragraph illustrates precisely the two kinds of combat involvement that I discussed earlier of the police. The very first sentence refers to "borbena dejsiva" in the original, which is correctly translated as "combat activities." And it then states that both active and reserve components of the police participated in the most intensive combat operations on the territory of a whole host of surrounding villages in the Prijedor region and that 11 employees of the police lost their lives and 25 of them were wounded in that. It then goes on to say that: "After these combat activities, employees of the police worked intensively on mopping-up operations," which the term here is "ciscenje terena" and this entailed the apprehension and detaining and subsequently interrogation of certain persons who had been identified as being connected with enemy activities on this territory. I would refer also to the following page, where there's a statistical chart, that I believe provides ample illustration of the extensive combat involvement of the police in the Prijedor municipality throughout the year. The cumulative total there is 16.602 days of -- those are man days of combat operations in the municipality alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in any event, were these the operations that in addition to whatever weapons were surrendered by the Muslim and Croat population resulted in the list of confiscated weapons that is contained as tab 32?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the -- the types of operations that were carried out during the -- the summer of 1992 and which resulted in confiscation of the aforementioned weapons, and they also resulted in -- as the report correctly notes, "the detention and interrogation of the aforementioned persons in the three detention centres" listed in the paragraph immediately following the statistical table to which I referred, that would be Keraterm, Trnopolje, and Omarska. I would also observe that this report reflects participation in combat and mopping-up activities that, according to previous reports of SJB Prijedor - and I referred earlier to some reports by Drljaca in May 1992 to Zupljanin - these were operations that resulted on at least one occasion, according to SJB Prijedor, in hundreds of deaths among the "innocent Muslim population." That was the term used by Drljaca in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just in relation to that, Your Honours, Mr. Tieger in his question indicated: "In any event, were these the operations that in addition to whatever weapons were surrendered by the Muslims and the Croat population resulted in the list of confiscated weapons that is contained at tab 32?" The question in and of itself contains an assumption of evidence that is not, in my submission, borne out by the documents, and that is "surrendered by the Muslim and Croat population." If one looks at tab 31, precise information in relation to devices confiscated by paramilitary formations, if one looks at -- and there's no delineation there. If one looks at tab 32, there's a list of weaponry. If one goes to the report again, in and of itself, it does refer to mopping-up activities; but then again at the same time there have been orders extant in the time -- at the time of paramilitary formations being disarmed, be they Muslim, Croat, or Serb. And in the circumstances, Your Honours, Mr. Tieger's question contains an assumption in relation to the evidence that should not be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's very helpful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, were the ciscenje operations reflected in Mr. -- in the Prijedor report directed against Muslim villages or Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am certainly no expert on the demographics of villages surrounding Prijedor. I know that there were villages that were predominantly Muslim there; I also know that there were a number of villages that were of a predominantly Serbian population. What I can state for certain is that the names of some of the villages that are contained in the report that we just looked at - that is to say, the report on the work of the Prijedor Public Security Station during the last nine months of 1992 - include the names of the villages that Drljaca referred to in May 1992 when he referred to "hundreds of deaths of the innocent Muslim population."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the people who were rounded up and brought to Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje, do the documents reflect whether they were to an overwhelming extent one ethnicity or another? And I'm referring to being rounded up and brought to Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje during those operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just ask, Ms. Loukas: I take it that your objection was not aiming at -- or was not based on any doubt as to the ethnicity of those detained in Omarska --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour. I think that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. That's clear --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we have -- we have --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- misunderstood the nature of my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that Ms. Loukas thought the weaponry mentioned in tab 32 might well have been from paramilitary units from whatever -- whatever ethnicity. At the same time, Ms. Loukas, there is quite a lot of evidence which refers to hunting rifles, which were mainly the weapons that were in the hands of the locals, to say it that way. Well, it's -- if I look at that list, and if I compare what I would need to arm a paramilitary unit, and if I compare it to what is described as usually in the hands of ordinary citizens, then it comes closer to the letter than the first. The matter is not sufficiently important to -- to spend a lot of time on it. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, I agree, Your Honour. But nevertheless, I -- it is a marker to ensure Mr. Tieger does not include matters that are not established by the evidence

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I say "let's proceed," then it's because I think we wasted some time. So let's then do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But this does include a hand-held rocket launcher, Your Honour. It's not just about hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, do you know whether disarming operations by the Bosnian Serb MUP were directed primarily against one ethnic group or the villages of one ethnic group or formations of one ethnic group or another?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police documents that I've been able to review, in particular the police documents from the Autonomous Region of Krajina that we've been focussing on here, overwhelmingly suggest that those disarming operations focussed on Croats and -- and in particular Muslims in North-Western Bosnia. That is not to say, however, that there are no documents in which evidence is provided that weapons were confiscated from Serbs. Such documents are indeed also available, but the number of those documents and the number of weapons confiscated from Serbs in those documents is of a much lower quantity than the numbers of weapons confiscated from Muslims. It would also be important to observe in this connection that the confiscation of weapons and the implementation of the aforementioned disarming orders often, according to the police reports, involved large-scale combat operations followed by mopping-up operations coordinating with the VRS in which houses or on some occasions entire villages were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm assuming we're going until quarter to 3.00, based on the time that we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We are at -- almost at one hour and a half. So if this would be a suitable moment for a break, we'd then --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is as good as any, I'd suppose, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is as good as any other. Then we'll adjourn until ten minutes past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, there are a few procedural matters I'd like to deal with, and I don't think that -- although it may be boring for the witness, his presence, I think, would not be a major problem. The first is that I created confusion by not reading out the whole of the decision on the fifth batch of 92 bis witnesses, which makes the -- the handout incomprehensible in respect of witness Nikola Samardzic. I'll now read out that part of the decision which I inadvertently left out. I wanted to say that: "I now turn to Witness Samardzic. Having read the material proposed for admission, the Chamber has decided not to admit the statement or the attachments. The Chamber will, however, give an opportunity to the Prosecution to further explain the relevance of this material, and the Chamber may thereafter reconsider its decision." That also explains why in the handout items admitted says "none" in respect of Mr. Samardzic. That's the first issue. The second issue is the Chamber received a -- at least, the three Judges of the Chamber received a letter, Mr. Krajisnik, which is dated the 3rd of June. That's today. And I take it that it is a response to our invitation to write down a few subjects that could be discussed during the meeting you suggested. I am informed, although I have no formal translation of this letter, that although it explains why you'd like to have a meeting, it does not give the subjects you'd like to discuss. And in order for those who will be present to know exactly -- who should be present, who is involved in the matters or not, you are again invited to write down, even if it was on a piece of paper - just point 1, this, point 2 that, point 3, that - to write that down so that those who feel that they should attend that meeting are at least aware of what it is about. Of course, the letter will be translated, but I thought I would tell it to you now. Then the third procedural item is the following: And that, Mr. Nielsen, does concern you in some respect. This afternoon we'll continue with the examination of Mr. Nielsen, the cross-examination. I don't know how much time you'd still need, Mr. Tieger, but certainly the testimony will not finish today. Then the question is whether according to the originally agreed schedule that we would have Monday and Tuesday off and then restart at Wednesday or whether - Ms. Loukas, I'm especially also looking at you - whether you'd prefer to finish with the witness and then perhaps find some relief at the -- then later. The Chamber has no -- not a very specific point of view, apart from some commitments, I think mainly on the 6th. But I'd like to know what the parties would like to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Well, first, of course, I don't know how much longer is in the examination-in-chief, but regardless of that, there's -- there's no question that I would finish today. So therefore there's a question of whether we continue on Monday, which I'm happy to do, or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Ms. Loukas speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, the microphone is looking in a different way as from where you stand.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Often these machines have a mind of their own, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the question. Yes, that's the question, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Your Honour, in those circumstances, of course, there's a matter I raised with Your Honours in the absence of the witness, of course. I guess there's a question of whether the cross-examination is completed on Monday or at some other stage. And in those circumstances, I'm perhaps a little circumscribed in relation to what I might say in view of the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps then we deal with it at the end of this hearing, or what's --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Perhaps the --

utterances.text: We could ask the witness to --
