utterances.text: Perhaps at the end of the evidence in chief, I think, Your Honour, might be appropriate, or if the witness might leave. The other question is, of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I should raise that as well. Is this question of -- Your Honour indicated at the end of the proceedings yesterday in relation to the question of the further argument on the question of Mr. Krajisnik's self-representation and some time being set aside at the -- either the beginning of today or at the end of today in relation to that question. And I understand that Mr. Harmon and Mr. Stewart have been in communication with each other on that question, and I -- I understand that some 45 minutes have been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, at the end of this -- today, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: At the end of today, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just have a look. Let's -- let's proceed at this moment. And at the end of this session we'll hear from you in the absence of the witness what you'd like to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, I wanted to return to some -- to at least one of the questions that was posed earlier, I believe, by Judge Hanoteau concerning your analysis of various reports. And I think you'd referred to dozens of reports that you had an opportunity to review of internal MUP reports. And I wanted to know whether that was a reference to the daily bulletins that have been addressed or a reference to the 90 various individual reports which were sent to the Prime Minister and the president and members of the -- and the 80, excuse me, various reports on the security issues which were sent to the president and members of the Presidency that is -- that was discussed yesterday and is contained -- is reflected in the annual report.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My earlier reference to dozens of reports that I had had an opportunity to -- to review was a specific reference to the MUP daily bulletins and the bulletins that were feeding into those daily bulletins, coming from the CSBs. The total number of documents that I've had an opportunity to review is, of course, much, much larger than that and includes many other types of documents from the MUP. With respect to the 90 reports and the 80 reports cited in the draft annual report, I've never seen any list produced by the Ministry of what exactly those reports are. I can only speculate, and I think with good reason, given what we have seen in handwriting on the cover of the 17 July report earlier today, that that would be one of the reports that is part of the 80 or 90 reports cited in the draft annual report. However, I am unable to say how many of those reports cited in the draft annual report I have been able to review.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I noted that during your -- during the last session you were obliged to explain to the Court the area of concentration to which you devoted your attention and the areas of focus for other members of LRT. I apologise for that. That was, I think, my mistake and not more painstakingly permitting you an opportunity to describe to the Court precisely what you focussed on in drafting your report and in contrast to other members of the LRT, and I should probably give you that opportunity now. Was -- so was your focus on the Ministry of Internal Affairs? Was your focus on the government? Was your focus on the Presidency? Can you describe the area to which you specifically devoted your attention.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the entire period of my employment with the leadership research team, I was specifically tasked to focus on the RS Ministry of Internal Affairs. During the second year of my presence in the leadership research team, that ambit was expanded to include the Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs, that is to say, the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Serbia, and the Federal Secretariat for Internal Affairs, also located in Belgrade. However, I was not tasked specifically to review the documents concerning the functioning of the RS government or Presidency or, for that matter, the Crisis Staffs. As has been the practice throughout the existence of a leadership research team, I was, of course, aware of the areas of competence of my fellow colleagues. I consulted with them regularly on matters on which they were experts. And they regularly made me aware, as I did for them, of documents from their areas of competency that might be relevant to my area of competency. This, for example, would be the case with the Presidency and government sessions where the person or persons responsible for working on that issue would as a matter of course let me know whenever the Ministry of Internal Affairs was discussed in sessions of those bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of the report here, as the title suggests, it is restricted to the establishment and performance of the Bosnian Serb Ministry of Internal Affairs in the period from approximately November 1990 until the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you conducted an analysis of the internal documentation of the RS MUP primarily or -- in contrast to the documentation relating to the Presidency, Assembly, government, and so on.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I would like to remind the Court of paragraph 6 on page 9 of my report in which I specifically lay out the focus and source base for this report. I would just note that in addition to examining the copious amount of documentation possessed by OTP with respect to the RS Ministry of Internal Affairs, I was also relying for the pre-April 1992 period on documents produced by the SRBiH MUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I had indicated earlier that I hoped to move quickly through the material, and I still intend to do so, so I have relatively few questions left. I wanted to ask you first about that portion of your report that deals with what happened to the Muslim and Croat members of the joint MUP in the municipalities where Serbian authorities took power. And your report deals with terminations and loyalty oaths. I think yesterday you mentioned a commendation to Mr. Kovac for reducing the numbers of Muslim members of the police so that by the time of the outbreak of the war there were none. Were there other areas where the -- and other SJBs where the members of the -- Muslim or Croat members of the MUP were disarmed or discharged?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were. The ethnic composition of RS MUP changed quite dramatically during the first months and was certainly radically different from the ethnic composition of the joint MUP in the period previous to April 1992. It is difficult to describe that process in a simple manner because the documents produced by RS MUP suggest that what transpired in the SJBs and in the CSBs varied considerably from municipality to municipality. That is to say, in some cases - Ilidza is one example - it appears, based on RS MUP's own documentation, that already at the outset of April 1992 there were only Serbs and a handful of Croats employed in that public security station. In other municipalities, such as Pale and Sokolac in the Romanija region, there had also been moves to reduce the number of Muslims working in the public security stations there prior to April 1992. However, in still other municipalities - for example, Kljuc or Prijedor - numerous Muslims remained working in the police throughout the month of April 1992, and it was only at the end of April or in some cases even later in May that the Muslims in those municipalities ceased to work in the police. The manner in which they ceased to work and whether or not they were given an opportunity to take an oath of loyalty to the new MUP, again, varies municipality by municipality and in some cases even within the municipality from police station to police station. What is perhaps the most important statement that can be made on this topic, however, is that the outcome of the personnel movements, which I have tried to describe very briefly, is clear by the end of June 1992. I would refer to paragraph 199 on page 59 of my report in which I quote: "A quarterly report of RS MUP which stated that by the end of June 1992 for the entire Ministry of Internal Affairs of the RS there were only six Muslim employees and all the others were Serbs." That is to say, no Croats and only six Muslims in the entire ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask you a question on that topic, which runs as follows: We can see that there's been a reorganisation of the police. We also see that those people of Muslim faith will no longer be part of these police forces. So this new police system, is it a police system which has the same head count as before or are people being newly hired to offset those people who are going to be leaving, and how are these people going to be hired? I'd like to know whether all of this was well prepared. Were there any instructions given? And if that was the case, how was this actually implemented?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll answer the question on the numerical composition of the RS MUP first. And the answer, to the best of my knowledge, based on the documents, is that the overall number of persons employed by the ministry - more information can be found in the report to which I just referred as well as the draft annual report - is that the police actually increased in size, in number of employees, despite the fact that large numbers of police officers of Muslim and Croat ethnicity left the ministry for various reasons that are laid out in my report. To the question as to whether all of this was well prepared and how these people were being -- where the new people came from, the documents that I've been able to review again suggest a great deal of improvisation at the local level. The Chamber will no doubt recall my reference yesterday to Bosanska Krupa municipality in which the Belgrade secret police service had already received information of an informal Serbian militia or Serbian police of Bosanska Krupa. In many municipalities for which we have documentation the recruitment process seems to have been taking place first covertly, as the report yesterday in Zvornik suggested, and then later more overtly, where military-aged Serbs were -- who were not already in military units were being gathered into formations that would later become part of regular police units. Indeed, it is in this particular instance particularly, I think, useful to refer back to the Security Day parade that we discussed earlier in the special police unit of CSB Banja Luka. That -- the composition of that unit came largely from a previous paramilitary force known as the Serb defence forces, the SOS, that had been quite active in the Krajina region. We also see an admission, which I quote, from the Minister of Internal Affairs at, I believe, it's the 22nd Assembly Session in November, on the 23rd and 24th of November, 1992. I may have to search a little bit to find the correct passage. The gist, however -- I can paraphrase before I find the immediate quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I can be of assistance, I think that's at paragraph 203, reference to the 22nd Session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. At the 22nd Assembly Session, Mico Stanisic, the Minister of Internal Affairs, looking back at the beginning of the war, says: "Because there was a reserve element at the beginning" - this is a quote - "we wanted the country to be defended. They took thieves and criminals, because I ask you, no doctor of science emerged with a rifle in his hands to defend this country nor any intellectual. That was our priority task. We had good intentions. Perhaps we erred in this respect. I allow for that." And this is, in fact, an acknowledgment made by Stanisic which is reflected in other police documents that the persons recruited into the police force, and in particular special police units, such as the police unit in Banja Luka to which I referred, came from backgrounds that were by the police themselves and their own documents known to be of a criminal nature. Indeed, again, in the case of Banja Luka, Stojan Zupljanin as early as September 1991, half a year -- well over half a year before the formation of RS MUP, himself referred to the proliferation of paramilitary groups formed by Serbs in the SAO Krajina region. And the documents that I've been able to review suggest that some of the same people to which he referred in his communication were later recruited into the police force or cooperated in joint operations with the police as a -- paramilitary formations. I should note that the communication of Zupljanin to which I refer was a letter that he sent, I believe, on the 23rd of September, 1991 and the letter was addressed to Biljana Plavsic, Miodrag Simovic, Momcilo Krajisnik, and, I believe, one member of the military at the time. And Vitomir Zepinic as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, I don't think I understood your last part of the answer correctly. When you mentioned this letter, which was sent to so on and so forth, what -- what was this letter about? I didn't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This particular document is -- is a letter that I do not cite in my report but I am happy to produce it for the Trial Chamber. I have the -- the ERN handy, but it is in my binders and I reviewed it in the context of preparing for this testimony. The document is a report in which Zupljanin, who was also at that time the chief of CSB Banja Luka for SRBiH MUP, explains quite pressing concerns that he has about the deteriorating security situation in North-Western Bosnia. In particular, he refers to a proliferation of armed paramilitary groups and he states that these groups are openly affiliating themselves with political parties. Indeed, in the case of the SDS, he notes that some of these paramilitary groups have begun to provide security for SDS rallies that are taking place in North-Western Bosnia. And what he essentially asks the addressees is what can be done at the Bosnian level about this deteriorating security situation and, in particular, about these groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this letter, does he express concerns about the unreliable way in which these people are being hired or the way in which these policemen are being hired? Is he worried about the fact that the security situation is due to the fact that some people have been hired without paying particular attention to who these people are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that point in time in September 1991, events have not yet reached the stage that these persons are being hired by the police. So that is not a specific point of Zupljanin's concern. His concern is that these persons - and I recall one in particular from the document, Veljko Milankovic, who would later lead a group called the Wolves of Vucjak - had formed a group of armed men who were quite well-armed, indeed in some cases better armed than the local police in the Bosnian Krajina, and that Zupljanin had been able to verify that Veljko Milankovic and others in this group and other group had significant criminal dossiers; that is to say, they had been previously prosecuted on numerous occasions. And things were at that juncture - that is to say, September 1991 - reaching a stage that Zupljanin felt that the police would not be able to act if events escalated further because they were, in fact, outarmed by these political -- by these paramilitary groups which had explicit political affiliation. And I wanted to link that, as I do in the report on page 64, to the later integration of the paramilitary Serbian defence forces into the special police unit of CSB Banja Luka. In effect, it's a contrast between the position taken apparently by Zupljanin in September 1991, where he was very concerned about this, and in April 1992, where he is now willing to integrate some of these units into his own police force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry to take all the time dedicated to the Prosecution, but I'd like to understand the following: When on a local level people who did not meet the usual standards were called upon, was it the result of local initiatives without referring to higher levels, or was all this -- was all this procedure the outcome of instructions that had been given previously? Were these initiatives reported to higher levels? Because this was quite an unusual development. Well, at least I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can only comment on the police recruitment as it's reflected in the documents of both SRBiH MUP and RS MUP. In the pre-war period, it needs noting that all three ethnicities in SRBiH MUP, the Croats, the Serbs, and the Muslims, mutually accused each other on regular occasions of trying to integrate paramilitary units or paramilitary components into the MUP. For example, the Muslims were alleged to have taken a large number of Muslim males from Sandzak and to be equipping them as police officers using irregular procedures; that is to say, circumventing the proper hiring procedure that's laid out in the laws and regulations affecting the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Once the war starts, the procedure, as I -- or the -- the actual events, as I've been able to see them in the documents of RS MUP, suggest that a significant amount of pre-war recruitment had gone on on a covert basis, and once the war started, much of this was at a local level. I do not see any specific instructions on how these persons should or should not be hired or what the criteria for that should be, given to the ministry or for that matter the municipal SJBs from higher authorities. What can be observed, if we refer back to the 11 July meeting in Belgrade, is that by the time that we get to midsummer of 1992, the minister and several of the heads of CSBs are quite concerned about the intervention of local authorities in, and in particular Crisis Staffs, in the day-to-day running of the police and in certain appointments, who will be the commander, who will be the chief of police in a given municipality. And one of the main conclusions coming out of that meeting is to try to ensure that the police will operate properly, including in hiring procedures. With respect to the persons who are already in the ministry and who may have committed acts that are disciplinary or criminal violations, Mico Stanisic issues an order in the course of the summer of 1992 in which he specifically says that those people will be removed from the Ministry of Internal Affairs and placed at the disposal of the VRS. That is, they will go and participate in VRS operations. And I believe we have that document in the binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just one last question about the loyalty oaths. And in that connection, if I could ask you to turn to tab 28 of binder 2. Tab 28 contains the conclusions of the -- of a meeting of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina from May 18th, 1992. If I could ask you to turn your attention to conclusion number 8. It states in the English: "Loyalty of other nationalities to the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina should not be only verbal." First of all, based on your reading of the original, is there any translation issue that needs to be addressed before identifying that particular topic or discussing that particular conclusion?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having examined both the original in B/C/S and the English version, I believe we have a discrepancy, an important discrepancy between the translation and the original. I believe -- my reading of -- of point 8 is that -- the following: "The loyalty of other nations of the Serb -- to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina cannot be of an only declarative character."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in line with the Court's instructions, perhaps you could read the original and that will provide the courtroom interpreters an opportunity to interpret it for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last few words of that line would do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Must not be of declarative character only."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the significance of that conclusion, then, Mr. Nielsen?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular point relates to the loyalty oaths that are being administered in -- to police officers throughout the Serbian Republic at this point in time. And it is essentially stating that merely declaring loyalty orally or in a writing, on a certificate or an oath, is not sufficient by itself or in and of itself to demonstrate loyalty to the Serbian Republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke about a request for reporting on certain crimes related, if I recall correctly, to vehicles or oil. With respect to the reporting of crimes required by the -- that was required by the Ministry of the Interior, the Serbian Ministry of the Interior of its members, was there any emphasis in the documents that you were able to review on crimes against one ethnicity or another?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case, I would like to refer to paragraph 238 of my report, on page 71, in which I discuss Minister Stanisic's response to the government's request dated 24 May, and that was the request that we examined and discussed yesterday. I already noted that the document we saw in which Stanisic asks for specific information from the CSBs specifically mentions the theft of vehicles from the TAS complex at Vogosca and also the theft of oil from Ilidza. In addition, however, Stanisic also requested that information be provided on serious -- serious crimes committed against Serbs in territories controlled by the MUP of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina; that is to say, crimes against Serbs who were currently on territory not controlled by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the course of your review of the documents, did you encounter other -- any other references to reporting of crimes specifically committed against Serbs?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have mentioned earlier in my testimony the National Security Service of the RS. One of the main tasks of the National Security Service was to report on crimes committed against Serbs, again, on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina controlled by Muslim or Croat forces. That was something that was reported by them regularly to -- to the minister and to the under-secretary for National Security.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think I have one last question, Your Honour, but I need to look at a document first. [Microphone not activated] No, it's fine, Your Honour. And that concludes my questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Ms. Loukas, you suggested that we would hear you at the end of the examination-in-chief on the matter, which should be dealt with in the absence of the witness, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher -- Mr. Nielsen, may I ask you just to leave the courtroom for a second so that we can hear the submission by Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Two points in essence, Your Honour: Firstly, of course, I did place on the record at the commencement of this witness's evidence the situation of the Defence. That's the first point. And I thought it appropriate in -- in answering Your Honour's question that I make reference to that. And, of course, the witness should not be present in court at that stage. Now, Your Honour, the -- the situation we find ourselves in, of course, is that whether I do or do not commence the cross-examination today is -- is a matter for Your Honour to decide, in essence, but I would make the point that it seems to me, in calculating the amount of time left, that we'd be looking at something in the order of half an hour, it seems to me, taking into account the next break, the 45 minutes for Mr. Harmon and Mr. Stewart and what have you. Of that approximate nature, it seems to me. Nevertheless, if Your Honour decides that despite the matters that I have indicated to Your Honours previously that I should commence, I can commence. That's the first point. The second point is, of course, there's therefore a question of the continuation of the cross-examination. And, Your Honour, obviously I'm not going to conclude in half an hour so -- and, of course, the Monday and Tuesday have been designated as compulsory days in relation to the two additional witnesses that the Prosecution have asked for. I think that's 681 and 682. So, again, Your Honours, I'm in Your Honour hands as to how the Court wishes to use Monday and Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it -- that was the question to the parties. I mean, you get two days off. That's clear. But if you say, I would rather do that after we've finished with this witness, or whether we take the two as scheduled, the Court is -- of course, we -- we kept a bit in the back of our minds that we might not be sitting on Monday and Tuesday, so therefore our agendas are perhaps not entirely free anymore, but we'd like to know what you'd prefer, and the extent to which we could meet your wishes is another matter, and we'd also like to hear from Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can proceed on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, would there be any problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I haven't had a chance to check with Mr. Hannis in this case with respect to the next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- scheduled witness, and that seems to me to be a significant issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course there is the issue - certainly there is - that this witness doesn't have to travel very long to return, and it would be less traumatic, I take it, if he's -- if he would have to wait for two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, if I may, we -- it may be best, and we're going to take a break relatively soon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that you discuss the matter with --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that makes more sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes Then we'd like hear from you after the next break -- if there is a next break, because the question was whether you start with --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If you're interested in hearing the Prosecution on that, Your Honour, I think it's completely appropriate to begin. This -- as I understand it from Ms. Loukas, she had essentially a full week to prepare for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think Ms. Loukas -- Ms. Loukas doesn't make the point that she could not start and she -- of course she --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- In general terms she has referred to it, but at the same time she wonders whether the time remaining is such that it makes any sense at all to start.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, if I may, we have been as zealous as possible and under tremendous pressure to use our time as efficiently as possible. A half hour is not negligible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Every minute counts, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Absolutely every minute counts. But I really -- Your Honour, that's just silly on the part of Mr. Tieger, quite frankly. Because I've already indicated that I am happy to proceed for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, the Chamber is convinced that it will be more than half an hour, so you may proceed. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. So we'd like you to start with the cross-examination, which I think would take until approximately five minutes to 5.00. We would then have a 20-minute break, and the parties should limit themselves strictly to the time then remaining for the discussions on representation. We would then start approximately quarter past 5.00 with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger and Ms. Loukas, it's important for the organisation to know before 5.00 whether we'll sit on Monday or not. Of course, it asks for quite a lot of preparation. So even if you'd need two or three minutes to see whether it would be on Monday or whether on Wednesday that you would -- or take the necessary action to be prepared for making a final submission two minutes before 5.00 or preferably five minutes before 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, welcome back in court again. You'll be confined by Ms. Loukas, counsel for the Defence. Ms. Loukas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Ms. Loukas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Nielsen.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you prefer Mister or Doctor Nielsen?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mister is fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, just going to your report. First of all, when was it first indicated to you that you would be writing this report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived at ICTY -- my first day here was June 16th, 2002. And on that particular day, already on the very first day it was explained to me that I would be working on the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the RS. I believe the Chamber might recall that was during the phase when certain other reports that -- in particular the Bosnian Serb leadership report of Mr. Treanor, around the time that that was filed, and there was a perceived need in the Office of the Prosecutor for an additional report on the Ministry of Internal Affairs. I was therefore asked to work on this particular topic that forms the body of this report, and I believe that the actual notion of filing a report, as opposed to merely conducting research on it, and filing a report for this case was, to the best of my knowledge, taken in a decision that was taken in September or October of -- of 2002.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Nielsen, were you given terms of reference in relation to what was required --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, before you proceed, I noticed already from the first answer, which was an answer to a very short question, when was it first indicated to you that -- you didn't stop the witness, which is fine if you think that all the details are of the relevance -- of such relevance that you would not stop the witness. On the other hand, Mr. Nielsen, Ms. Loukas just asked when. She has the habit of asking further details if she needs them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please start focussing your answer on the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then if further details are needed, you'll certainly be asked to give them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, getting back to my second question. Were you given terms of reference in relation to what was required of you in relation to this report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were they written or oral?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were oral.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were those terms of reference?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The terms of reference were to produce a report on the Bosnian Serb Ministry of Internal Affairs that would fill, again, the perceived gap left by other analytical reports produced by the leadership research team and by the military analysis team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what precisely was that perceived gap, Mr. Nielsen?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The perceived gap was the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Serb Republic. Although the other reports prepared by other experts in the Office of the Prosecutor certainly touched upon the Ministry of Internal Affairs in passing, there was no expert report that focussed in-depth on the functioning and the establishment of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're now, of course, at the ICC, the International Criminal Court, and I think you left here in August of 2004. That period from your commencement in June 2002 until August 2004 with the Office of the Prosecutor and the legal research section, did you spend the entire two years on -- on this report for research and research around this area?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never worked for a legal research section. It was the leadership research team of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, that's -- I misspoke there. The leadership research section. It's -- "legal" does come rather quickly to the mouth of a lawyer, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. I filed the original version of this report, as the version in front of us indicates, in December 2003. I then continued to update it based on new documents that were still arriving at OTP. And I filed the final version on my last day at work, which was the 13th of August, 2004.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during this -- this time, Mr. Nielsen, did you have consultations with the Prosecutors in this case?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had contact with the Prosecutors in this case on a very frequent basis. Sometimes on a daily basis, sometimes on a less frequent basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did these contacts involve?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These contacts most frequently involved requests by the Prosecutors for specific information pertaining to the MUP, to the RS MUP, or to SRBiH MUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've said "most frequently involved." What other sort of consultations did you have with the Prosecutors in this case?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also had contact with the Prosecutors in this case with respect to participation in missions to the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of missions?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I undertook a series of missions as a research officer to obtain additional collections of documents pertaining to RS MUP from various archives in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in that connection I had contact with the Prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've quite fairly indicated, Mr. Nielsen, that your expertise is in the area of the Ministry of the Interior, as opposed to the government, the Presidency, the Crisis Staffs. Your area of expertise was quite specialised in that regard; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 6 of your report, you indicate that -- it's not an exhaustive analysis of all the aspects of the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina between November 1990 and the end of 1992. You've indicated there that you've -- you've incorporated relevant articles from the contemporary press. What was your process of selection in that regard?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the press articles specifically or in general?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'll come to the others, but specifically in relation to your press articles.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Office of the Prosecutor, there are a large number of press articles that have been registered with ERNs, and I had access to those press articles. And when I did encounter articles that dealt specifically with SRBiH MUP or RS MUP, I read them and included them if I believed that they added significantly to the information that was contained in -- in the RS MUP and SRBiH MUP documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in relation to what you've indicated right at the beginning of paragraph 6 there, that -- that you've made an analysis of documentary material, how was the review and selection made of these documents that you're referring to there in paragraph 6? Was it done by you? Was it done by others in the section? Or can you just describe for us how this process of selection in relation to the documentation was made.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. The primary way in which documents were selected for this report was through my reading and analysis of a much larger group of documents, and from that larger group of documents the selection was made. I was in the majority -- in fact, the vast majority of cases the person who identified the article and decided to include it. In other cases, to which I've alluded earlier, my colleagues, who worked on other aspects of the Bosnian Serb Republic or indeed other aspects of events in the time of Bosnia and Herzegovina, made me aware of articles that seemed to them to be relevant to RS MUP or SRBiH MUP and then presented these articles to me. In all cases, however, I was the sole arbiter of which documents would be cited in this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in -- in making that decision, as the -- the sole arbiter, were you keen to -- I take it you were keen to ensure that you included documents that didn't just go toward establishing a Prosecution theory but, rather, being an impartial expert.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mention only briefly in your report this question of Variant A and B. I think you make mention of it at paragraph 44 and again at paragraph 59 of your report. You -- you know the paragraphs that I am dealing with there, Mr. Nielsen?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, of course, you can't offer the Court any more than what you've examined from the -- the documents in that regard; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to that particular aspect. Were you aware of correspondence between Mr. Blewitt, the Deputy Prosecutor at the time, writing to the Republika Srpska Serb Democratic Party on or about July 2001?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that. I was not employed by ICTY at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in your --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm referring now, Your Honours, to Defence Exhibit D9, and I have copies. I might present it to the witness to see if it ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Rings a bell.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Rings a bell. Indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll give you a moment to have a look at the -- the letter from Mr. Blewitt and the response from the -- the response in relation to that letter. I take it, Mr. Nielsen, you've now acquainted yourself with that particular exhibit?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I think you've indicated in your evidence that, of course, within your unit there would be discussions, for example, with Mr. Treanor and Ms. Hanson in relation to your respective areas of research; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you would bring documents to each other's attention; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in view of the fact that you were in your report at some point dealing with Variant A and Variant B, did Mr. Treanor ever bring this document to your attention?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time that I have seen this set of correspondence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So therefore I take it you were not aware that Mr. Treanor was referred to this letter, in fact, during his cross-examination in April of 2004, prior to your leaving this establishment?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did follow part of Mr. Treanor's cross-examination, but I did not follow the part in which this particular exhibit was discussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, going on to specific mentions that have been made of Mr. Krajisnik in your report. And, of course, you'll recall that Judge Hanoteau also asked you some questions in this regard. And I am referring specifically to paragraphs 74, 75 of your report. You recall the paragraphs that I'm referring you to, Mr. Nielsen?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have them in front of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's in relation, of course, to the 11th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly held on the 18th of March, 1992. Now, you refer there to the fact that Mr. Krajisnik referred specifically to the need for "ethnic separation on the ground." And then you follow that sentence immediately with: "Miroslav Vjestica, an SDS delegate from Bosanska Krupa referred to the need for the establishment" -- and I might slow down, I think, for the interpreters because I'm tending to read a little fast there. "... establishment of a Serbian police force and a Serbian MUP so that Serbian -- so that Serbs could seize control of their territories." Now, just to go to the actual Assembly session on the 18th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I sent an e-mail this morning indicating that I would be using this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we are prepared for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're prepared for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have the Assembly session in front of you now, Mr. Nielsen?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now -- as I think was agreed the other day, what was on the agenda there, of course, was dealing with the latest session of the conference on solutions for the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the political situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Yugoslavia. And in essence, of course, what was under discussion there was the most recent bout of international negotiations involving the Cutilheiro Plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when one looks through the session - and I'm now referring to page 6 of the English version - reference is made to the fact that -- the question of the three constituent units which is part of the agreement for further negotiations, of course. And when one looks at page 8 - and I think this is in the -- the midst of Mr. Karadzic's introduction on this topic - again, in the context of what's proposed for all three constituent units, towards the bottom of page 8: "We will be in charge of the police, trade, and other aspects of economic policy." Again, that's a reference to what would be the case for each constituent unit, that being the Bosnian Serb unit, the Bosnian Croat unit, and the Bosniak or Muslim unit; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, sorry, Your Honour, but if there's a suggestion that this is part of the agreement itself, it -- it covers a lot of ground and certainly encompasses a portion of -- of Mr. Karadzic's remarks when he starts -- when he leaves the text and starts explaining what the future intentions are. So either the witness has to know if it's a reference to the specific -- to any specific document or a reference to Mr. -- to Dr. Karadzic's remarks.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, as Mr. Tieger has said, the witness is an expert. The witness is more than aware of the Assembly session. And the witness has spent something like two years examining these documents. If he can't answer a question like that with Mr. -- without Mr. Tieger seeking to protect him, I'm a little concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's avoid words as "protection." I mean, it doesn't add anything to -- I quite understand, Ms. Loukas, that you're unhappy if Mr. Tieger interferes in this way and you think the witness could answer the question. Let's try to intervene as -- if -- if not really necessary, and I don't think it was really necessary and there would have been an opportunity to ask further questions in re-examination, if needed. Ms. Loukas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Nielsen, do you remember my question?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't need to repeat it, so -- and if you need time to review the -- the document, take your time.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm certainly not an expert on the Cutilheiro Plan or the history of the Cutilheiro Plan or the international negotiations going on at this point in time. But with respect to the specific portion of the minutes - and I believe that I stated something quite similar yesterday - at this particular juncture there was contemplation that there would be an ethnic separation in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that the three main ethnicities in Bosnia and Herzegovina would each have their own police force with respect to that specific question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Nielsen. Now, further along, again, this is at page 10, just before Professor Koljevic speaks, again in reference to the negotiations that have been carried on under the auspices of the -- of the European Community, a statement is made that "Bosnia-Herzegovina is divisible along ethnic lines and it can be divided in three units." Again, Mr. Karadzic is talking about the basis for the negotiations that had been successful thus far; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic is talking about a set of negotiations or a process of negotiations that is ongoing, and as he states at the outset, and as -- as is later stated by Mr. Krajisnik in the same session, "The Bosnian Serbs believe at this juncture that immediately following this round of negotiations they have made significant advances."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Nielsen. Now -- and again, if you move on to page 12 of the session in question, where Mr. Krajisnik speaks. He's obviously positive about the negotiations; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to a particular paragraph or in -- in general?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In general.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There -- there is a -- a bit of -- of, I think, one could call it, optimism in this session among the participants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he also, I think, indicates at the top of page 13 that "Since municipality borders may be adjusted, we have already made some adjustments and we plan to include all parts that will be Serbian territory in our municipalities and what remains to be discussed, the discussion will be about where it's going to be and where we are going to put our lines." And, again, that's a reference to the ongoing negotiations about how the -- the SDA, the SDS, and the HDZ are going to draw their lines on these three constituent units; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this particular case, it's a specific reference for -- to the fact that the Bosnian Serbs have already at this point been starting to contemplate what lines they wish to draw with the expectation that that map, as is later stated in the session, that map or maps in general on national division have to be discussed at a future negotiation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed. Now, Mr. Nielsen, and when you go to the bottom of page 13, and we're there dealing with the specific quote that you've taken from the session, and that is "ethnic division on the ground," where he says after that sentence that "We start determining the territory, and once the territory is determined, it remains to be established in additional negotiations whose authorities are to function and in what way." It's quite clear, isn't it, that when he talks about "ethnic division on the ground" and the use of the term in the next sentence "additional negotiations" that the ethnic division on the ground is contemplated in terms of a negotiated settlement in contemplation of the Cutilheiro Plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a bit lost because I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there's a mistake. The quote was on the bottom of page 12.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At any rate, I'll deal with it in the English --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. My copy has page 13 for some reason. So I'm one page ahead.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at this stage, yes, he says that there will be additional negotiations surrounding the determination of territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- and again, a few paragraphs down, he basically is giving the Assembly his impressions and saying that he was very pleased after the -- these talks and much more pleased than he was after Brussels; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is a particular pleasure expressed, as I noted yesterday, that the Bosnian Serbs believe that the European Union or European Community at that particular time has now agreed to accept some kind of ethnic separation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in relation to that, there's just -- again, there's a further comment from Mr. Krajisnik after Dragan Djokanovic [phoen] finishes speaking, and Mr. Krajisnik refers to the fact that it's in this -- this latest agreement for the basis of negotiations on the Cutilheiro Plan, that part of the agreement is in relation to the various constituent units having special relationships with whatever that -- republic they want to. You know, the Bosnian Croats having a special relationship with Croatia; the Bosnian Serbs having a special relationship with Serbia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He does not aggress -- address the Bosnian Croats. He only says that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, indeed. I'm just --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the Bosnian Serbs are entitled to have free links of any type with Serbia and Montenegro and anyone that they may wish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed. And, of course, what was contemplated in the Cutilheiro Plan, that was the same for all ethnicities, for all three constituent units; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm forced to state that I'm not familiar with the terms of the Cutilheiro Plan, other than as they are discussed in the Bosnian Serb Assembly session. So I can certainly state what it is that the various speakers said about the plan, but whether that is actually in the plan is not something I'm in a position to comment on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- and subsequently you have Dr. Karadzic speaking just before Ljubo Bosulja [phoen] - and I'm sure your pronunciation is much better than mine - but he's making the point there that "We have to establish a full structure of government on the ground because this is our duty to the people who live there, Serbs, Muslims, or Croats, so that we can have peace." Do you see that portion I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And interestingly enough in the discussion by Mr. Perisic in the third final paragraph of the discussion of Mr. Perisic, his contribution, just above the contribution of Rabija Subic.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I ask for a page reference, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On mine it's page 28, but I think on yours it might be page 27.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He makes a comment there about the fact that -- do you see the sentence I'm talking about? "Why do you not ask Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Ursic [phoen] about their ability to have some influence when support or cooperation of the organs with executive authority municipalities, it is almost non-existent"?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Ms. Loukas slow down a little bit for the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, if you would have had your headphones on, then you would have heard the request by the interpreters to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: The request by the interpreters, Your Honour ...? Oh, to slow down a little bit, yes. I'm just trying to get as much done in the limited time I have available, Your Honours. But I do take the point. It's just that I find with the headphones that after a while they start hurting my ears. I don't know. It's -- so I try to ... but I'll keep them on for the rest of the period, I think, and try to slow down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, moving on, Mr. Nielsen. There's a -- a Mr. Karovic, which appears on my page 31, which is probably your page 30.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karovic doesn't seem to be very happy. He's indicating that he's basically not happy with the negotiations. He's saying, "We have not done anything." And -- and then thereafter Mr. Krajisnik appears to be trying to calm him down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm waiting for a question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, the question is: You'd agree with me he's trying to calm him down in that regard. That's a fair reading of the -- the Assembly session?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He -- he does state that Mr. Karovic's comments, he seems to think they're -- that he needs calming down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's -- and it's quite clear from this discussion thus far that Mr. Krajisnik comes across as somebody who's -- who believes in the negotiating process and the international negotiations that are preceding. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've stated previously, Mr. Krajisnik at this particular session believes that the latest round of negotiations have brought a positive development for the Serbian people and that is in concurrence with what the Assembly wants, and he believes that these negotiations will continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, again, just after Mr. Krajisnik speaks, at that point we have got a Mr. Goran Zekic, who again is expressing dissatisfaction with the negotiating approach, and he's basically saying, "All negotiations will continue and Bosnia-Herzegovina will exist as an internationally recognised entity that will keep postponing to deal with internal arrangements for a decade." Do you see the -- the portion where Mr. --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Zekic speaks on the bottom of my page 33, and I think that's probably your page 32.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And again Mr. Krajisnik, he -- he responds to this negativity in relation to negotiating by saying, "What can I hear -- what can I say after hearing Zekic. It's as if we had not discussed anything, as if he had just entered the room."

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see that passage. And I note that Mr. Krajisnik also said that nothing was agreed as yet, that this was all working material.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed. And he also says towards the -- the end of what he has to say in response to Mr. Zekic's negative contribution that -- "Can we hear only the concrete proposals, please." And again, it seems, does it not, that Mr. Krajisnik is still emphasising the importance of the negotiating sphere; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he certainly wants to solicit concrete proposals with respect to the negotiations rather than negative emotions regarding the most recent evolution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we go to Mr. Vjestica's contribution, which is at the bottom of my page 36, which I think would be the bottom of your page 35; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, I'm looking at the clock. We are going to stop at five minutes to 5.00. We still have the outstanding issue to be resolved before 5.00, whether we'll proceed on Monday or not. I therefore suggest that we leave Mr. Vjestica for next session, whenever that may be.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Perhaps it might be also appropriate to find out from the witness his availability as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nielsen, we'll discuss at this moment when we'll proceed. I think there are -- Ms. Loukas, there are a few options. And Mr. Tieger, I take it that you'll find out also about the next witness to arrive. What we could do is to continue Monday and see how far we come, and then restart anyhow on Wednesday with Witness 679, and then have another day -- a free day or another day off where you could prepare for -- for the witnesses for which these additional days have been given. That's an option. Another option is just to take the two days off and to restart on witness -- on Wednesday. Whether that would be with Mr. Nielsen or with someone else would then still have to be decided. These are, I think, the -- the most -- the most likely options to -- Mr. Tieger, you have tried to find out about ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Our recommendation is to resume on Monday, then take Tuesday and Wednesday off, and on Thursday we can begin with the next scheduled witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that be -- yes. You're half dressed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I actually came in at the last minute because I was watching the screen and realised there was discussion about scheduling, and I came down specifically with something to offer on the topic. So I came straight in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART

utterances.text: Yes. I would say start negotiations with the Prosecution to see whether that problem can be solved, Mr. Stewart. We'll adjourn until 18 minutes past 5.00.
